references.text: Describes how the Lord used a strong east wind to divide the sea, which is the background for God blowing with His wind and the water covering the Egyptians.
Tells how the waters returned and covered the Egyptian army, Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen, so that they sank into the sea.
Parallel description in the same song where the Egyptians sank into the depths like a stone, corresponding to the comparison with lead in verse 10.
Uses similar imagery about God's breath (nesah) revealing the bottom of the sea and uncovering the foundations of the earth.
Describes how God sends His word and His wind (ruach) to carry out His will, parallel to God blowing with His wind.
Speaks of the Lord's breath (ruach) that blows and causes the grass to wither, an image of God's powerful breathing.
Refers to the same event at the Sea of Reeds where the pursuers were cast into the depths like a stone in mighty waters.
Describes God's breath (neshamah) as a powerful instrument that can destroy, similar to the motif in Exodus 15:10.
Thematic parallel linking the Red Sea to creation mythology and God's victory over chaotic powers.
Contrastive parallel: the same wind that saves Israel in Exodus is used to destroy the enemy (Tyre) in Ezekiel.
Direct parallel to the same event (the Red Sea) focusing on God's ability to make the water stand like a wall.
Prophetic retelling of the same event (the Red Sea) focusing on God's military intervention through the sea.
Thematic parallel: the use of storms and tempests as God's instrument to pursue and terrify enemies.
